newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech bourse chairman sees watchdog in autumn.
newsitem.headline: Czech bourse chairman sees watchdog in autumn.

text.p: The Czech Republic should have a functioning independent stock exchange oversight body by autumn of this year, Prague Stock Exchange (PSE) Chairman Tomas Jezek said on Thursday.

Speaking to journalists at a capital markets regulation conference, Jezek also said he would present his proposals for a U.S-style securites and exchange commission (SEC) to parliament by the end of this month.
"At the end of March we will put it to the parliament, and then it depends on parliament how long it takes...(I hope) by the second half of this year, the autumn," he said.

Under the proposals, the SEC will be headed by a board of five members elected by parliament but it will be financed independently of the legislature via fees drawn from a percentage of each transaction made on the bourse.

In contrast with neighbouring countries, notably Poland which has had a capital market watchdog for over six years, the Czech capital market has been overseen by a poorly-staffed department in the Finance Ministry which has only limited powers.
As a result, the Prague bourse has earned a reputation among foreign investors as lacking transparency, rampant with insider trading and short of protection for minority shareholders.

"There's been a very definite cost to their not having proceeded in the line of some reasonable regulation of the market place," said Richard Smith, a former commissioner of the U.S. SEC who has been helping Jezek prepare his proposals.
"And I think it's quite evident that a number of international investors just won't come to the Czech market now," he added.
The Czech Republic developed the most highly-capitalised bourse among the post-communist countries of central and eastern Europe after two waves of mass voucher privatisation in the early 1990's.

The process was led by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, an avowed disciple of Milton Friedman and Margaret Thatcher, who has shown little sympathy for calls to strengthen regulation of the capital markets.
Asked whether he thought Klaus would now be more supportive of his efforts to create a Czech SEC, Jezek said: "I hope so."
